Rare endocannabinoid system variants identified by whole-exome sequencing and structural modeling in adults with severe obesity predominantly of childhood onset.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The endocannabinoid system (ECS) regulates key processes in energy homeostasis, but its contribution to severe obesity beginning in childhood or adolescence remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to identify rare variants in ECS genes and evaluate their potential structural effects.
METHODS: A total of 93 adults with severe obesity beginning before 21 years of age (BMI ≥ 35 kg/m²) were recruited from two specialized obesity programs; among participants with onset information, 97.8% reported childhood onset. Whole-exome sequencing was performed, followed by targeted analysis of ECS-related genes. Rare variants (allele frequency <1%) were confirmed by Sanger sequencing and assessed using in silico pathogenicity prediction and molecular modeling. In silico saturation mutagenesis of all 19 possible substitutions at each variant position was additionally performed using three complementary stability predictors based on different methodological principles (FoldX, Pythia and DDMut), together with AlphaMissense.
RESULTS: Nine rare variants were identified in twelve individuals, seven of which were defined as variants of uncertain significance (VUS). Among the observed variants, FAAH p.(Arg326Pro) showed the most concordant predicted impact: it ranked as the most destabilizing substitution at position 326 by FoldX (ΔΔG = +3.04 kcal/mol; rank 1 of 19) and was the only observed variant classified as likely pathogenic by AlphaMissense (0.884). Arg326 lies 24.3 Å from the catalytic triad (Lys142-Ser217-Ser241), consistent with a predicted effect on fold stability rather than direct disruption of the active site. Conversely, at DAGLA position 750, all 19 substitutions were predicted as neutral by FoldX and DDMut and as likely benign by AlphaMissense, consistent with predicted structural tolerance at this position. No anthropometric or metabolic parameter differed significantly between carriers and non-carriers after correction for multiple testing.
CONCLUSIONS: Rare ECS variants, including a previously unreported FAAH p.(Arg326Pro) substitution, were identified in adults with severe obesity, predominantly with childhood onset. These in silico analyses are predictive and provide computational evidence for prioritizing candidate variants, notably FAAH p.(Arg326Pro); they do not, by themselves, establish pathogenicity or a causal relationship with the phenotype, which will require functional validation.

title: Clinical characteristics and genotype-phenotype correlation analysis in 279 patients with 5α-reductase type 2 deficiency.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: 5α-Reductase type 2 deficiency (5α-RD2) is an autosomal recessive differences/disorders of sex development caused by SRD5A2 gene mutations, characterized by impaired testosterone-to-dihydrotestosterone conversion and highly heterogeneous clinical phenotypes. The genotype-phenotype correlation of 5α-RD2 remains incompletely understood, and large-scale multicenter evidence is lacking for clinical management.
METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, CNKI, Wanfang, and Chinese Medical Journals databases from inception to December 2025. A total of 279 genetically confirmed patients with 5α-RD2 from 36 countries (64.77% from Asia) were included. Demographic, clinical, biochemical, genetic, and prognostic data were extracted and analyzed using SPSS 25.0.
RESULTS: Seventy-eight pathogenic SRD5A2 mutations were identified, with missense mutations being the most common (64.10%) and p.R246Q the most prevalent variant. The mutation spectrum showed significant geographic heterogeneity. Consanguinity was strongly associated with homozygous mutations (P < 0.001), and patients with homozygous mutations had significantly more severe undermasculinization than compound heterozygotes (P = 0.011). p.R246Q, p.G203S, and p.R246W were significantly associated with a higher likelihood of hypospadias; p.R227Q was significantly associated with a lower likelihood of cryptorchidism and scrotal abnormalities. Frameshift mutations were associated with impaired pubertal development (P = 0.013). Homozygous carriers were diagnosed significantly later than heterozygotes (P = 0.029), and serum FSH levels positively correlated with phenotypic severity (P = 0.021).
CONCLUSION: We verified that the genotype-phenotype correspondence is non-linear and multifactorial, jointly modulated by mutation subtype, residual enzyme activity, endocrine axis status, geographical disparities, consanguinity, and regional medical resource availability. These findings provide more reliable evidence for clinical diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis assessment.

title: Up to 5 years of weekly somatrogon in children with growth hormone deficiency: final data from the global phase 3 study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This open-label extension (OLE) study aimed to evaluate the long-term efficacy and safety of once-weekly somatrogon in pediatric patients with growth hormone deficiency (GHD) following up to 5 years of somatrogon treatment.
METHODS: Patients who had previously completed 12 months of treatment (somatrogon or somatropin) in a phase 3, randomized, active-controlled study (NCT02968004) were eligible to enroll into this OLE study; somatropin-treated patients were switched to somatrogon (0.66 mg/kg/week), and somatrogon-treated patients received somatrogon at their previous dose.
RESULTS: A total of 212 patients entered the OLE. Mean annualized height velocity at the end of OLE Year 1 (Y1), Y2, Y3, and Y4 was 8.11, 7.91, 7.02, and 6.56 cm/year, respectively. Mean height SDS increased in each year of the OLE and approached 0 SDS by OLE Y4. Mean (SD) IGF-I SDS was positive and within the normal range throughout the OLE. The incidence of adverse events (AEs) was 53.8% to 72.3%, with most being mild to moderate. The incidence of serious AEs in each year was low (0-4.7%), and none were related to treatment. The most common treatment-related AEs were injection-site pain and injection-site erythema. The presence of antidrug antibodies did not appear to impact safety or efficacy outcomes.
CONCLUSION: Based on the final data from the largest cohort of somatrogon-treated patients to date, once-weekly somatrogon demonstrated sustained efficacy and an acceptable safety profile during the OLE period. Once-weekly somatrogon constitutes a valuable long-term alternative to once-daily somatropin, offering potentially improved adherence and treatment outcomes.

title: Overt and subclinical hypothyroidism during pregnancy: effects on neonatal amino acids, acylcarnitines, and TSH levels.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Maternal hypothyroidism during pregnancy, including overt and subclinical hypothyroidism, is a common endocrine disorder complicating pregnancy and is associated with increased risks of adverse maternal and fetal outcomes. However, its effects on neonatal metabolism remain inadequately understood. This study aimed to assess the association between hypothyroidism in pregnancy and neonatal amino acid and acylcarnitine levels.
METHODS: This retrospective case-control study included 1,987 pregnant women with overt hypothyroidism in pregnancy, 2,023 with subclinical hypothyroidism in pregnancy, and 2,043 euthyroid pregnant women from Fujian Provincial Maternity and Children's Hospital between 2016 and 2024. Their newborns all underwent newborn screening for 11 amino acids and 31 acylcarnitines using tandem mass spectrometry.
RESULTS: After adjusting for potential confounding factors including gestational age at delivery, birth weight, and neonatal sex, newborns born to mothers with hypothyroidism in pregnancy (overt and subclinical) showed significant differences in the levels of 9 amino acids compared with those born to mothers with normal thyroid function. These amino acids are involved in the arginine-proline metabolism, glycine metabolism, and the urea cycle pathway. Amino acid levels also differed between the two subtypes. In addition, the levels of short-chain, medium-chain, and long-chain acylcarnitines in newborns from the hypothyroidism groups were significantly higher than those in the control group, with several acylcarnitine indicators (C16, C16:1, C16OH, C18:1OH, and C6DC) exhibiting characteristic differences between the two subtypes. The levels of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in newborns from both hypothyroidism groups were significantly higher than those in the control group, whereas no statistically significant difference in TSH levels was observed between the overt and subclinical hypothyroidism groups.
CONCLUSION: Our findings revealed a significant association between hypothyroidism in pregnancy (overt and subclinical) and neonatal amino acid and acylcarnitine levels, which were mainly involved in branched-chain amino acid, arginine, proline, and glycine metabolism, as well as the urea cycle and fatty acid oxidation pathways. These results underscore the importance of identifying maternal conditions that correlate with neonatal metabolites, providing a reference for exploring strategies to optimize neonatal nutrition and improving long-term health outcomes.

title: How can we best distinguish rapidly progressive from slowly progressive precocious puberty in girls?
Exploratory secondary analysis of published aggregate growth and metabolic data in children born small for gestational age treated with growth hormone.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To describe published annual growth and metabolic summaries for children born small for gestational age (SGA) treated with growth hormone and to define the limits of inference from aggregate registry data.
METHODS: We conducted an exploratory secondary analysis of published aggregate means, standard deviations, and outcome-specific sample sizes from baseline through year 5 in the SGA subgroup of the Korean LG Growth Study, with up to 318 children represented at baseline. Primary reporting was descriptive and included annual values, changes from baseline, and measurement availability. Exploratory slope models were retained only as supplementary sensitivity analyses. The published aggregate LGS summaries available for the present secondary analysis did not include longitudinal blood-pressure measurements or cardiovascular-event records.
RESULTS: Height SDS was -2.38 at baseline and -0.76 at year 5, weight SDS was -2.21 and -0.84, and BMI SDS was -0.93 and -0.64. The published mean AST was 32.07 IU/L at baseline and 24.28 IU/L at year 5, whereas several other metabolic markers had higher year-5 means. Median year-5 measurement availability was 12.8% of outcome-specific baseline counts, and only six triglyceride measurements were available at year 5. The markedly reduced outcome-specific sample sizes at later follow-up points substantially limit interpretation of long-term patterns.
CONCLUSION: Published annual mean values differed across follow-up, but changing outcome-specific samples and the unavailability of individual-level longitudinal data to the present secondary analysis preclude estimation of within-child change, causal treatment effects, or cardiovascular risk.

title: Clinical and Molecular Genetic Testing Risk Stratification for Pediatric Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma Therapy.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Children and young adolescents with papillary thyroid cancer (CAYA-PTC) have high recurrence rates. Current guidelines advocate intensive treatment, yet existing risk stratification systems lack integration of genomic characteristics and provide limited precision in guiding surgical extent and postoperative radioactive iodine (RAI).
PATIENTS AND METHODS: This retrospective, multicenter study analyzed 435 CAYA-PTC patients (ages 2-18 years) treated between 2006 and 2024. A clinicogenomic nomogram for disease-free survival (DFS) was developed using clinical data, postoperative pathology, and molecular testing of surgical tissue. Patients were stratified according to the nomogram score. Model performance was internally compared with the American Thyroid Association (ATA) pediatric risk system. Treatment associations were assessed by surgical extent (total thyroidectomy vs lobectomy) and receipt of postoperative RAI therapy within each risk stratification.
RESULTS: Five variables were independent predictors of worse DFS: age ≤15 years, tumor size >4 cm, lateral neck node involvement (N1b), coexisting Hashimoto thyroiditis, and RET/NTRK fusions (all P <.05). The nomogram stratified patients into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups with 7-year DFS rates of 92.4%, 83.1%, and 56.4% (P <.001). In internal comparison, nomogram-based risk stratification had higher concordance index (0.721 vs 0.656) and 3-year AUC (0.748 vs 0.651) values than ATA stratification (both P <.05). Total thyroidectomy was associated with better DFS in intermediate- and high-risk patients but not low-risk patients. Higher DFS with postoperative RAI was observed in the high-risk group (P =.028).
CONCLUSIONS: Using retrospective clinicogenomic features, our stratification suggests a risk-adapted framework for CAYA-PTC. However, non-significant differences, especially in small subgroups, do not establish treatment equivalence or confirm the safety of de-escalation. These findings represent associations that require future external validation.

title: Serum FGF-21 levels and stature in children and adolescents with celiac disease on a gluten-free diet.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate stature in patients with celiac disease (CD) adherent to a gluten-free diet (GFD), determine the prevalence of growth hormone deficiency (GHD), and assess the associations between stature and serum insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 3 (IGFBP-3), and FGF 21 levels.
METHODS: In this prospective cross-sectional study, 141 pediatric patients with CD (79 females) who had adhered to a GFD for at least 2 years were included. Anthropometric and clinical data were obtained from medical records. Serum IGF-1, IGFBP-3, and FGF21 levels were measured in fasting samples. Growth hormone stimulation tests (L-dopa and clonidine) were performed in patients with a height >1.5 SDS below target height (TH).
RESULTS: Twelve patients (8.5 %) had persistent short stature despite long-term adherence to a GFD. Growth hormone deficiency was diagnosed in three patients (2.1 % of the entire cohort; 25 % of patients with persistent short stature). Patients with persistent short stature without GHD had significantly lower serum IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 standard deviation scores than those with normal stature, whereas serum FGF21 concentrations did not differ significantly between the groups. Serum FGF21 concentrations were not significantly correlated with height SDS, IGF-1, IGFBP-3, or other anthropometric variables.
CONCLUSIONS: Persistent short stature may occur despite long-term adherence to a GFD in a small proportion of children and adolescents with CD. GHD was identified in 2.1 % of patients, emphasizing the importance of growth monitoring. Lower IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 SDS in patients with persistent short stature without GHD suggest alterations within the GH-IGF axis. Serum FGF21 concentrations were not associated with stature, suggesting that persistent growth impairment in treated CD is likely multifactorial and is not explained by circulating FGF21 alone.

title: Somatrogon versus somatropin in children with growth hormone deficiency: a real-world matched-cohort study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Somatrogon is a once-weekly growth hormone (GH) analog approved for GH deficiency (GHD), but real-world head-to-head data are limited. Using a matched-cohort design with a protocol-defined IGF-1 sampling time, we compared first-year growth outcomes and safety of somatrogon and daily somatropin in children with GHD.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective matched-cohort study in 30 children with GHD (15 per group) at a single center. Groups were matched by age (±1 year), sex, and pubertal stage. Annual height velocity (AHV), height standard deviation score (SDS) gain, insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) SDS, insulin-like growth factor binding protein 3 (IGFBP-3), bone age advancement, and metabolic parameters were assessed at 12 months.
RESULTS: AHV was similar in both groups (8.96±1.67 vs 8.84±1.57 cm/year; p=0.841). Height SDS gain did not differ (0.60±0.36 vs 0.53±0.33; p=0.569). IGF-1 SDS was numerically higher in the somatrogon group (+0.59 vs -0.14; p=0.132) but remained within safe limits in all patients. Bone age advancement, glucose, and insulin levels were similar between groups. No adverse events or injection-site reactions were documented during follow-up.
CONCLUSION: In this matched cohort, no significant differences in growth or safety outcomes were observed between somatrogon and somatropin at one year. Somatrogon appears to be a reasonable alternative to daily GH therapy in children with GHD.

title: Cortisol Cutoffs for Adrenal Insufficiency Using Elecsys II: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Adrenal insufficiency (AI) is associated with increased risk of morbidity and mortality if improperly managed. Adrenocorticotrophin (ACTH) stimulation testing is the most widely used AI diagnostic test. Historically, a serum cortisol threshold of 500 nmol/L (18.1 µg/dL), derived using polyclonal assays, was widely used. Improved monoclonal immunoassays show reduced cross-reactivity and lower cortisol values, but no universally accepted ACTH-stimulated cortisol threshold exists. Suggestions ranging between 348 and 485 nmol/L [12.6-17.6 µg/dL] reflect methodology and cohort differences. Our objective was to systematically review the literature and recommend a revised cortisol threshold.
DESIGN AND METHODS: We searched MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for English language studies published between January 2016 and 19 September 2023 (PROSPERO CRD42023479405). Eligible studies reported original data, used the Roche Elecsys II assay, and recommended a cortisol threshold. Quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE framework, and risk of bias with the ArRoWS questionnaire. Multiple suggested thresholds based on ROC, sensitivity/specificity, or regression analysis were identified.
RESULTS: Six studies involving 1799 samples from 430 adult and paediatric patients were included. A serum cortisol cutoff of 405 nmol/L (14.7 µg/dL) was defined based on synthesis, sensitivity analysis, and a conservative approach to reduce false‑negatives.
CONCLUSIONS: We affirm recommendations to lower the cortisol threshold for AI when using monoclonal assays. A peak threshold of 405 nmol/L (14.7 µg/dL) is suggested for a standard-dose ACTH test on the Elecsys II assay for diagnosis of AI, acknowledging limitations related to the small number and GRADE quality of included studies.

title: Permanent congenital hypothyroidism with GBP1 p.Leu187Pro: clinical follow-up data and epigenetic insights.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: GBP1 variants have recently been identified as a novel cause of congenital hypothyroidism (CH), but the clinical spectrum remains incompletely defined. Longitudinal data on methylation dynamics at cg12054698, an open-sea CpG site within the GBP1 5' untranslated region (5' UTR), and normative methylation levels in euthyroid controls are lacking.
METHODS: We identified three unrelated CH probands carrying the heterozygous GBP1 p.Leu187Pro variant by trio whole-exome sequencing and systematically screened 61 known CH-related genes. Clinical phenotypes and longitudinal outcomes data were collected. For epigenetic analysis, cg12054698 methylation was quantified by pyrosequencing in the three probands, their carrier parents, 30 age-stratified euthyroid controls (newborns, toddlers, and adults), 10 CH patients without GBP1 variants, and paired longitudinal samples from two probands.
RESULTS: All three probands presented with moderate-to-severe CH at neonatal diagnosis. Thyroid ultrasonography revealed heterogeneous phenotypes, including a normal in situ gland, thyroid agenesis, and a normal-sized gland with diffuse hypoechogenicity. All three cases were confirmed as permanent CH. In euthyroid controls, cg12054698 methylation was significantly higher in newborns than in toddlers and adults (p<0.001). Neonatal methylation levels did not differ significantly among probands with GBP1 variants, CH patients without GBP1 variants, and euthyroid controls (p=0.260).
CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, GBP1-associated CH was permanent and showed a marked phenotypic heterogeneity. cg12054698 was hypermethylated during the neonatal period across study groups, supporting a developmentally regulated, stage-specific epigenetic pattern rather than a disease-specific pathogenic "second hit."

title: Weight Maintenance Following Discontinuation of Semaglutide in an Adolescent with Antipsychotic-Associated Weight Gain: A Case Report.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Antipsychotic-induced weight gain (AIWG) presents a significant clinical challenge in pediatric psychiatry, often leading to Class II or III obesity and metabolic comorbidities. While treatment with metformin is the current standard of care, its efficacy is often modest. Preclinical and translational data suggest that, by targeting the underlying cause of AIWG, GLP-1Ras may help restore satiety signaling that is disrupted in patients taking antipsychotics.
CASE PRESENTATION: We describe an adolescent who experienced profound weight gain following aripiprazole treatment which was successfully managed with semaglutide. Notably, after achieving therapeutic goals of normalization of body mass index (BMI) and hemoglobin A1c, the patient was able to discontinue semaglutide while maintaining her weight loss and normalization of hemoglobin A1c over six months of follow-up.
CONCLUSION: This single case raises the hypothesis that GLP-1RAs could serve as a temporary "bridge therapy" to counteract iatrogenic metabolic insults; given the confounding factors discussed below, this observation is hypothesis-generating and requires confirmation in larger, prospective studies before broader clinical application.

title: Thyroid Abnormalities in a Prospective Longitudinal Cohort of Pediatric Patients following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
abstract: Introduction Thyroid dysfunction has been reported in adults and children following COVID-19. We evaluated thyroid function in children following SARS-CoV-2 infection compared to uninfected controls over at least one year of follow up. Methods Thyroid function tests (TSH, Free T4) were analyzed in pediatric participants enrolled in the Pediatric SARS CoV-2 Long Term Outcome Study (PECOS), a diverse, prospective, longitudinal, multicenter cohort study. Assessments were conducted at baseline, and at follow-up visits for both infected and uninfected cohorts. Results Among 505 participants with non-missing data at baseline and 12-months, no significant differences were noted in proportion of TSH or Free T4 abnormalities among the infected vs. uninfected participants. Among infected participants 5% (25/464) developed subclinical hypothyroidism (high TSH and normal free T4) following recovery from SARS-CoV-2 infection, compared with 4.9% (2/41), a similar proportion in the uninfected group (p=1). Within the infected subgroup during 36-month follow up, three were treated with levothyroxine for persistent TSH elevation or goiter and 2/3 had positive thyroid antibodies consistent with autoimmune thyroid disease. Neither the number of SARS-CoV-2 reinfections nor number of COVID-19 vaccination status predicted the occurrence of TSH abnormalities. Conclusion Children infected with COVID-19 did not have increased thyroid dysfunction compared to uninfected controls during 12 months of follow up. A small proportion (5%) developed mild subclinical hypothyroidism that was transient in both groups, and only 3 infected participants (with TSH>10mcIU/mL or thyromegaly) needed levothyroxine replacement after 36-month follow up in this subgroup. Risk of thyroid autoimmunity compared to the uninfected population needs further study.

title: Pediatric Inpatient Continuous Glucose Monitoring: Development and Implementation of a Hospital Policy for Accuracy-Validated Insulin Dosing.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: We assessed the safety, clinical accuracy, glycemic outcomes, user outcomes, and implementation of a pediatric hospital-wide continuous glucose monitor (CGM) policy.
RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: We used the Model for Improvement to develop a pediatric hospital policy supporting CGM-based insulin dosing with accuracy validation using capillary finger-stick blood glucose (FSBG) and then retrospectively evaluated the program's clinical effectiveness and implementation outcomes with the Simplified Implementation Logic Model to connect contextual determinants, support strategies, and outcomes.
RESULTS: From September 2024 to October 2025, 60 people with diabetes used the CGM policy in 93 hospital encounters, including 46.7% (28/60) people with type 1 diabetes and 38.7% (36/93) encounters with automated insulin delivery use. The most used CGMs were Dexcom G7 (49.5%) and Abbott Libre 3 or 3 Plus (31.2%). Accuracy validation using the %20/20 criteria was successful in 81.5% of attempts, and the mean absolute relative difference was 12.6%, with 1207 paired CGM and reference FSBG values. Nurses responded appropriately after 97.8% (218/223) of failed CGM validation attempts. CGM time in range (70-180 mg/dL) was 54.8%, and time in level 2 hypoglycemia (<54 mg/dL) was 0.8% for the 58 out of 93 encounters with complete CGM data downloads. Nurses preferred using CGM with policy support instead of FSBG for insulin dosing (adjusted P = 0.046). Factors contributing to nursing preference included ease of use, system integration, and the ability to learn the system quickly.
CONCLUSIONS: We translated an inpatient CGM policy from an adult to pediatric hospital setting, supporting high levels of protocol adherence, clinical accuracy, safety, and improved experiences for clinicians. Program evaluation informs connections between contextual determinants, support strategies, and outcomes of implementing a hospital CGM program. These data offer a roadmap for implementing pediatric hospital CGM at other centers.

title: Mild TSH elevation is independently associated with height in children.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To investigate whether mildly elevated thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) (<10 mIU/L) is associated with height in children independently of the growth hormone-insulin-like growth factor 1 (GH-IGF-1) axis, and to assess sex differences.
METHODS: This retrospective cross-sectional study included 2,447 children aged 2-10 years presenting for slow growth evaluation (2022-2024). Multivariable linear regression was used with adjustment for age, sex, and IGF-1 SDS; restricted cubic splines (RCS) were used to assess the dose-response relationship. Sex-stratified and sensitivity analyses were performed.
RESULTS: Mildly elevated TSH was present in 96 (3.92 %) children. Overall, TSH was inversely associated with height SDS (β=-0.03, p<0.001) independently of IGF-1; RCS confirmed linearity. The association was significant in boys (β=-0.03, p=0.002) and borderline in girls. Boys with elevated TSH had lower height SDS (β=-0.18, p=0.025). Sensitivity analyses: the association persisted after excluding low IGF-1 (β=-0.02, p=0.004) but not in children with short stature (height SDS ≤-2).
CONCLUSIONS: Mildly elevated TSH is independently associated with reduced height in children aged 2-10 years, independent of IGF-1. The association was significant in boys and borderline in girls, with no significant interaction. The absence of bone age and parental height data is a major limitation. These findings support growth monitoring rather than routine levothyroxine therapy.

title: Laboratory-based case finding using phosphate and alkaline phosphatase to identify genetic and nutritional rickets in children.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Hypophosphatemic rickets is a rare disease characterized by renal phosphate loss, leading to chronic hypophosphatemia, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and skeletal symptoms that may remain unnoticed until advanced stages. Early diagnosis is essential because effective treatment is available to reduce complications.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate a laboratory-based case-finding strategy for identifying oligosymptomatic patients with hypophosphatemic rickets using phosphorus and alkaline phosphatase results in a pediatric population.
METHODS: A descriptive observational study was conducted in patients under 18 years of age at a tertiary care hospital between June 2021 and July 2025. Of 47,127 phosphorus or alkaline phosphatase measurements requested, 45,923 measurements corresponding to 28,045 tests from 12,513 patients were analyzed after exclusions. Test showing hypophosphatemia and/or elevated alkaline phosphatase were identified, and X-rays and clinical data were reviewed for classification.
RESULTS: A total of 22,860 phosphorus measurements and 23,063 alkaline phosphatase measurements were analyzed, with both parameters available in 17,878 laboratory tests. Hypophosphatemia was observed in 2,281 phosphorus measurements (9.98%), and elevated alkaline phosphatase in 3,301 measurements (14.3%). Fifty-five laboratory tests (0.31%) from 37 patients simultaneously met the criteria for hypophosphatemia (<-2 SD) and elevated alkaline phosphatase (>+2 SD); 56.8% were male, with a mean age of 6.5 ± 6.0 years. Following clinical review, 15 patients (40.5%) were classified as having a bone mineral metabolism disorder, including 10 with osteopenia of prematurity, three with nutritional rickets, one with a pathogenic variant in PHEX, and one with osteoporosis in the context of ReNU syndrome; 10 patients (27.0%) were classified in the acute/critical illness group and 12 (32.4%) in the other category. Radiographs were available in 30 patients, with findings consistent with rickets in three (10%). One previously unrecognized case of mild nutritional rickets was identified.
CONCLUSIONS: Laboratory-based case finding using phosphorus and alkaline phosphatase may help identify pediatric bone metabolism disorders, including forms of rickets. Combined hypophosphatemia and elevated alkaline phosphatase may be useful for guiding etiological investigation. This approach may complement clinical evaluation and facilitate earlier diagnosis. Early identification is clinically relevant because treatments can modify disease course and reduce long-term complications in children with confirmed forms of rickets, when appropriate.

title: Evaluating the implementation of the Diabetes Body Project in a clinical cohort of Australian adolescents with type 1 diabetes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Adolescents with type 1 diabetes (T1D) are at increased risk of disordered eating behaviors (DEB) and eating disorders (ED) compared to their peers without T1D, contributing to increased diabetes-related complications, and elevated mortality risk. Despite this, there is a lack of targeted ED prevention interventions specifically designed for adolescents with T1D, within routine clinical care. The Diabetes Body Project (DBP) has demonstrated promising feasibility, acceptability, and reduction of DEB in young adults; however, its application in younger adolescents and real-world clinical settings has not been tested.
OBJECTIVE: This study aims to extend previous DBP research by evaluating its implementation within a real-world Australian clinical service. The study will assess feasibility and acceptability and explore preliminary efficacy in relation to DEB and glycaemic control in an exclusively adolescent population, including a novel parent/caregiver component.
METHODS: This protocol describes a pilot study that will recruit 24 female adolescents with T1D from the John Hunter Children's Hospital (JHCH) Diabetes Service in New South Wales, Australia, along with up to 24 parents/caregivers. Adolescents will participate in a 6-week virtually delivered manualised cognitive dissonance based DBP program, delivered in a group format across four cohorts of 6 adolescents. In addition, two group sessions will be developed and delivered virtually to parents/caregivers for each cohort. Outcomes will be assessed at baseline, post-intervention and at 3 and 6 months follow up. Feasibility will be evaluated through recruitment, retention, attendance, between-session activity completion and parent/caregiver uptake. Acceptability will be assessed via participant and caregiver satisfaction surveys. Preliminary efficacy will be explored through changes in disordered eating behaviors (Diabetes Eating Problem Survey-Revised), body appreciation (BAS-2), diabetes distress (PAID-T), and glycaemic outcomes.
DISCUSSION: This study will evaluate the implementation of an adapted DBP intervention for adolescents with T1D within a real-world clinical service. By incorporating a novel parent/caregiver component and targeting the adolescent population, the study addresses key gaps in current literature. Findings may inform the design of future larger-scale trials and support the integration of ED prevention strategies into routine pediatric diabetes care.

title: When diabetic ketoacidosis becomes a neurological emergency: cerebral edema in a child with new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus - a case report and narrative review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a life-threatening complication of type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1D), potentially leading to severe outcomes, including cerebral edema (CE). The case describes an eight-year-old child with previously undiagnosed T1D complicated by DKA, and subsequent development of CE. It is followed by a short literature review including other pediatric cases of clinically overt CE.
CASE PRESENTATION: A boy was admitted to the outpatient clinic with a several-day history of vomiting, abdominal pain and headache, leading to a presumptive diagnosis of gastrointestinal infection. The following day, the patient's condition deteriorated. Despite a positive family history of T1D (the patient's father), his blood glucose level was measured for the first time by the emergency medical service (25.6 mmol/L (460 mg/dL)). Further evaluation revealed DKA secondary to previously undiagnosed T1D. On admission, the boy was in severe general condition. Severe DKA was confirmed (pH 6.88), and appropriate treatment was implemented, resulting in temporary clinical stabilization. However, on the second day of hospitalization, the patient's condition deteriorated again. He was somnolent, with fluctuating consciousness and nuchal rigidity. An increase in intracranial pressure (ICP) was suspected. Optic nerve ultrasonography revealed increased optic nerve sheath diameters, also suggestive of raised ICP. Anti-edema therapy with mannitol was initiated based on clinical suspicion, resulting in clinical improvement. Dexamethasone and furosemide were administered as adjunctive therapy. Subsequent CT findings supported the diagnosis of CE. The patient was discharged after 10 days in good general condition.
CONCLUSIONS: DKA can be a diagnostic challenge for clinicians due to its nonspecific symptoms. Early signs suggesting this condition should not be underestimated, and bedside blood glucose should be measured early in children presenting with unexplained vomiting, weight loss, tachypnea, dehydration or altered consciousness. Close monitoring for complications is critical during treatment, especially for CE, one of the most serious and potentially life-threatening consequences of DKA.

title: Management of pregnancy in patients with Graves' disease secondary to alemtuzumab: a case series and literature review.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Alemtuzumab treatment for multiple sclerosis frequently induces Graves' disease (GD), characterized by common coexistence of stimulating and blocking anti-thyrotropin receptor autoantibodies (TRAb), causing fluctuations of thyroid function. Alemtuzumab-induced TRAb-positive hypothyroidism is also common. These conditions are challenging to manage during pregnancy, considering the imperative necessity to maintain euthyroidism to minimize risks for both pregnancy and fetal/neonatal outcomes.
METHODS: We reviewed the clinical course and therapeutic management of four pregnant women affected with alemtuzumab-induced GD or TRAb-positive hypothyroidism followed at our Institution, and seven additional cases published in literature.
RESULTS: At our institution two patients with alemtuzumab-induced GD (one diagnosed before pregnancy, the other during the third trimester) showed a good control of thyroid function on anti-thyroid drugs (ATD). Two women had alemtuzumab-induced TRAb positive hypothyroidism; during pregnancy thyroid function was partially controlled with levothyroxine (LT4) alone in one case, and fully controlled with block and replace (ATD and LT4) in the other case. No pregnancy or fetal/neonatal negative outcomes were observed, except for preterm delivery of a healthy baby in Case 3, due to emergency cesarean section for pre-eclampsia progressing to HELLP syndrome. The literature search showed seven additional cases of pregnant women with alemtuzumab-induced GD (N = 5) or TRAb-positive hypothyroidism (N = 2), mainly diagnosed during gestation, especially in the first trimester. Six newborns developed transient thyroid dysfunction, often requiring treatment and later resolved.
CONCLUSION: The clinical management of alemtuzumab-induced thyroid dysfunction during pregnancy is challenged by frequent difficult maternal biochemical thyroid control and TRAb-mediated fetal/neonatal thyroid dysfunction. These patients need to be managed in a specialist setting, with close monitoring of maternal thyroid function and fetal/neonatal parameters, especially in cases with high TRAb titers.

title: Diabetic cataract at type 1 diabetes onset: frequency and characteristics.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Pediatric diabetic cataract is a rare acute complication of diabetes mellitus and may result in permanent visual impairment. Reported prevalences range from 0.25 % to 3.4 %, while data from Germany remain limited. This study aimed to describe the prevalence and clinical characteristics of cataract in children with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes at a German tertiary medical center.
METHODS: We retrospectively evaluated children and adolescents admitted to the Department of Pediatrics and Adolescent Medicine, University Medical Center Ulm, with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes between January 2008 and February 2024 who underwent ophthalmologic screening at the Department of Ophthalmology of the same center. A final cohort of 141 patients was analyzed.
RESULTS: Cataract was diagnosed in 6 of 141 patients, corresponding to 4.3 % of the ophthalmologically examined cohort. The median age of patients with cataract was 12.4 years. Mean HbA1c was significantly higher in patients with cataract than in those without cataract (15.8 % vs. 12.4 %; p<0.05). Visual acuity was significantly lower in patients with cataract than in those without cataract (0.19 vs. 0.03 logMAR; p<0.05). The predominant morphology was snowflake-like posterior subcapsular cataract. Retinal findings were normal in all patients, irrespective of cataract status.
CONCLUSIONS: In this single-center cohort of screened children with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes, cataract was detected more frequently in our ophthalmologically examined cohort than previously reported. Pediatric diabetic cataract may be underdiagnosed at diabetes onset. Initial ophthalmologic evaluation in children and adolescents with new-onset type 1 diabetes should, therefore, include slit-lamp examination, especially in patients with visual symptoms or markers of prolonged hyperglycemia.

title: Alkaline phosphatase in paediatric practice: a practical approach with a proposed diagnostic algorithm.
abstract: This review summarises the clinical relevance of alkaline phosphatase (ALP) in paediatrics, placing emphasis on its biochemical heterogeneity, age-dependent physiology and diagnostic value in bone and hepatobiliary disorders. ALP is a group of membrane-bound enzymes, predominantly represented in serum by tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase, with major contributions from bones and the liver. In children, interpretation of ALP concentration is complicated due to marked physiological variation occurring in growth and puberty, as well as by method-dependent differences in laboratory reference ranges. An elevated ALP activity may reflect normal growth; however, it may also result from benign transient hyperphosphatasaemia, rickets, fibrous dysplasia, juvenile Paget's disease, metabolic bone disease of prematurity or cholestatic liver disease. Low ALP activity, although less common, may be associated with hypophosphatasia, malnutrition, micronutrient deficiencies or medication effects. ALP should, therefore, be interpreted in the context of age, clinical presentation and supplementary findings of biochemical tests and diagnostic imaging.

title: Assessment of central precocious puberty rates during the prepandemic, pandemic, and endemic COVID-19 periods.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Evaluate the frequency of central precocious puberty (CPP) diagnosis before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic.
METHODS: New patient referrals for precocious puberty among patients aged 1-12 seen at the Rainbow Babies and Children's Hospital's Pediatric Endocrinology Practice were analyzed during three separate periods: "pre-pandemic" between 7/1/2018 and 12/31/2019, "pandemic" between 7/1/2020 and 12/31/2021, and "endemic" between 07/01/2022 and 12/31/2023. Demographic characteristics were compared between time periods.
RESULTS: Of 6,162 new patients seen, 75 were confirmed to be idiopathic CPP. A significant increase in the total number of CPP cases compared to prepandemic levels was only seen during the pandemic period (p=0.038). Analysis across all three periods also did not reveal a statistically significant linear trend in the proportion of CPP cases (p=0.642). The median age of diagnosis was younger during the pandemic (7.7 years) compared to the endemic period (8.5 years), p=0.006, but no other demographic differences were found, including BMI.
CONCLUSIONS: Our study is the third single-center study in the literature to demonstrate the rise in the cases of CPP as a specific phenomenon to the pandemic period. Increase in stress during the pandemic is the most likely explanation for this transitory rise in the rates of idiopathic CPP.

title: Fatty liver and adipokines: converging pathways linking insulin resistance to early atherosclerosis in obese children and adolescents.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Childhood obesity drives nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and adipokine dysregulation, converging on insulin resistance (IR) to promote subclinical vascular injury measurable as increased carotid intima-media thickness (cIMT). Pediatric-specific mechanistic integration of these pathways with early atherosclerosis remains incompletely characterized. This review synthesizes evidence on NAFLD severity and cIMT in obese youth, examines the roles of resistin, high-molecular-weight (HMW) adiponectin, chemerin, and inflammatory mediators in IR-driven vascular remodeling, and evaluates their diagnostic and therapeutic implications.
CONTENT: A structured narrative review following SANRA guidance was conducted. PubMed/MEDLINE was searched from January 2000 to March 2025 for studies enrolling children aged 2-18 years with obesity and reporting cIMT measured by B-mode ultrasonography alongside NAFLD or adipokine measures. Quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) and AMSTAR-2. Across ten included studies (NOS scores: 5-8/9), obese children with NAFLD demonstrated consistently higher cIMT than controls (pooled weighted mean difference: +0.06 mm; 95% CI: 0.04-0.08 mm). Biopsy-proven nonalcoholic steatohepatitis independently predicted greater cIMT than simple steatosis (r=0.41; p<0.01). Resistin showed the strongest adipokine-cIMT association (r=0.47; p<0.001), with direct (β=0.31) and indirect effects via HOMA-IR (β=0.18) and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (β=0.12). HMW-adiponectin deficiency, rather than total adiponectin, defined the preatherosclerotic phenotype. Chemerin correlated with cIMT (r=0.44; p<0.01) and metabolic syndrome score (β=0.39; p<0.001). Weight-loss intervention reduced cIMT by 0.03 mm (p<0.05), accompanied by adipokine normalization.
SUMMARY AND OUTLOOK: NAFLD and adipokine dysregulation constitute interdigitated, IR-centered pathways associated with early atherosclerosis in obese youth, detectable from age 7 and partially reversible with timely intervention. A tiered algorithm incorporating BMI, liver enzymes, HOMA-IR, cIMT, and adipokine profiling is proposed for clinical risk stratification.

title: Iodine exposure and thyroid function after prophylactic intragastric iodinated contrast administration for meconium obstruction of prematurity in extremely low birth weight infants.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Maternal hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) increase the risk of meconium obstruction of prematurity in small-for-gestational-age (SGA) extremely low birth weight (ELBW) infants. While prophylactic intragastric amidotrizoate (Gastrografin®) promotes meconium excretion, concerns persist regarding iodine load and thyroid dysfunction.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed infants (<30 weeks, <700 g) born 2016-2024. The treated group (n=20) comprised SGA infants of mothers with HDP receiving prophylactic 5-fold diluted Gastrografin (iodine: 148-222 mg/kg) after stabilization. Controls included nontreated SGA infants (n=17), mostly lacking maternal HDP (thus not meeting prophylaxis criteria), and an appropriate-for-gestational-age (AGA) reference cohort (n=48). A 2018-2022 unexposed subcohort (n=21) provided baseline urinary iodine concentration (UIC) data.
RESULTS: Treatment failure, necessitating therapeutic enema, occurred in 1/20 treated infants (5 %). Baseline UIC was 32 (IQR 25-127) vs. 25 (IQR 25-35) µg/L in combined controls (p=0.23). Day 1 postadministration, UIC surged to 326,000 (IQR 201,500-455,350) µg/L; by 2 weeks, it normalized to 348 vs. 267 μg/L (p=0.51). At 2 weeks, thyroid function was comparable between treated and nontreated SGA groups for TSH (5.8 vs. 5.1 μIU/mL; p=0.94), free T3 (1.56 vs. 1.55 pg/mL; p=0.68), and free T4 (0.98 vs. 0.78 ng/dL; p=0.31), though baseline HDP differences necessitate careful interpretation. Levothyroxine supplementation rates were 26 % vs. 13 %, respectively (p=0.42).
CONCLUSIONS: Early postnatal iodine levels in preterm infants are low. Prophylactic intragastric Gastrografin facilitated meconium evacuation in high-risk SGA ELBW infants. The associated iodine elevation is transient. A nonsignificant numerical increase in levothyroxine supplementation within our small cohort necessitates further large-scale studies.

title: Performance of a 15-Day Continuous Glucose Monitoring System in Children and Adolescents With Diabetes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The CareSens Air (CSAir) continuous glucose monitoring system is approved for use in adults in South Korea and received adults-only CE marking in early 2024. The aim of this prospective, multicenter, pivotal study in children and adolescents with insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus was to determine if the performance and safety of CSAir in these populations are comparable to those observed in adults.
METHOD: Sensors were worn for 15 days on the upper arm in children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years and on the upper arm and/or upper buttock in children aged 2 to 6 years. Frequent capillary comparator measurements were performed during in-clinic sessions at the beginning, middle, and end of the sensor-wearing period. Point accuracy was assessed via agreement rates (AR) and mean absolute relative difference (MARD). Additional assessments included clinical point accuracy, technical reliability, and safety.
RESULTS: For subjects aged 7 to 17 years, %20/20 AR was 90.8%, and MARD was 8.9%. A total of 99.9% of values fell within Zones A and B of the Diabetes Technology Society error grid. Sensor survival probability reached 75.2%. In children aged 2 to 6 years, %20/20 ARs were 86.6% and 98.4%, and MARDs were 10.3% and 7.8% for arm- and buttock-worn sensors, respectively. No serious adverse events were reported. Mild and moderate adverse device effects comprised skin issues such as itching or erythema at the sensor application or insertion site.
CONCLUSIONS: The observed performance and safety of CSAir in children and adolescents are similar to those in adults. These data may support an extension of regulatory approval of CSAir for children aged 2 years and older.

title: Real-World Clinical Outcomes Following Initiation of the iLet® Bionic Pancreas in Youth with Type 1 Diabetes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The iLet® Bionic Pancreas replaces carbohydrate counting and manual bolus calculations with simplified qualitative meal announcements. Its performance among diverse patients with high baseline glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) is not well characterized.
METHODS: Retrospective, single-center cohort study of 71 patients aged 6-21 years with type 1 diabetes (T1D) who initiated the iLet Bionic Pancreas (2023-2025). Primary outcomes were changes in HbA1c and time in range (TIR; 70-180 mg/dL [3.9-10.0 mmol/L]) from baseline to 3 months. Secondary outcomes included glycemic metrics through 12 months, hypoglycemia, and meal-announcement behavior.
RESULTS: Mean age was 13.2 ± 3.5 years; 40.8% Black and 38.0% Medicaid-insured. Baseline HbA1c was 9.4 ± 2.1% (79 ± 23 mmol/mol) and TIR was 30.1 ± 19.0%. At 3 months, HbA1c decreased by 1.8 ± 1.7% (-20 ± 19 mmol/mol) and TIR increased by 22.4 ± 22.5 percentage points (both P < 0.0001) without increased hypoglycemia. Improvements were greatest among participants with baseline HbA1c ≥ 9.5% (≥80 mmol/mol) (ΔHbA1c = -3.0% [-32 mmol/mol]; ΔTIR = +31.2 percentage points). Among participants with paired 12-month data, HbA1c decreased from 9.6%-7.6% and TIR increased from 27.7 to 55.8% (both P < 0.0001). Mean meal announcements were 2.9/d at 3 months and 2.1/d at 12 months (P = 0.722) and were not associated with HbA1c or TIR at 3 months.
CONCLUSIONS: In this real-world pediatric cohort, iLet initiation was associated with substantial glycemic improvement without increased hypoglycemia, particularly among participants with high baseline HbA1c. Favorable outcomes were observed among participants contributing paired 12-month data.

title: Bone turnover markers in pediatric alkaptonuria: a case-control study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Alkaptonuria (AKU) is a rare inherited metabolic disorder characterized by progressive connective tissue damage and ochronosis. Although skeletal involvement is well documented in adults with AKU, data on bone metabolism during childhood are limited. This study evaluated bone turnover markers and mineral metabolism parameters in children with AKU.
METHODS: This cross-sectional case-control study included 16 pediatric patients with AKU and 27 healthy controls. Anthropometric measurements, serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase (ALP), parathyroid hormone, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, osteocalcin, β-C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (β-CTX), and urinary homogentisic acid (HGA)/creatinine ratio were assessed. Correlation analyses were performed between bone turnover markers, biochemical parameters, and urinary HGA levels.
RESULTS: Serum calcium concentrations were slightly lower in the AKU group than in controls (p=0.048), although values remained within the reference range in both groups. No significant differences were observed in anthropometric measurements, other mineral metabolism parameters, or bone turnover markers. Urinary HGA levels were not correlated with bone turnover markers. However, the urinary HGA to creatinine ratio showed a moderate negative correlation with body mass index (r=-0.61, p=0.02) and waist circumference (r=-0.58, p=0.02). In healthy controls, osteocalcin and β-CTX correlated positively with ALP and serum phosphorus, whereas these associations were absent in the AKU group.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that circulating biochemical markers of bone remodeling are preserved in children with AKU. Nevertheless, these results do not exclude early skeletal involvement and support the need for longitudinal studies incorporating additional biomarkers and imaging modalities to better characterize bone health in children with AKU.

title: A Genetic Risk Approach to Differential Diagnosis of Type 1 Diabetes and Risk Stratification in the Spanish Population.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Accurate type 1 diabetes (T1D) risk assessment can improve diagnosis and preventive care, reducing misdiagnosis and enabling preclinical interventions. Genetic Risk Scores (GRS) offer a promising tool, but population-specific validation is required.Objective. To assess the performance of established vs. a novel Spanish-specific GRS for T1D differential diagnosis and risk stratification.
METHODS: From 2,338 genotyped individuals, 2,215 Spanish participants of European ancestry passed quality control: 816 T1D, 469 type 2 diabetes (T2D), 457 monogenic diabetes (MD), and 473 controls. A novel Spanish-specific GRS (T1D-SP-GRS) was developed and compared with HLA-DRB1 and two European-derived models (T1D-GRS and T1D-GRS2). The best-performing score was evaluated for T1D discrimination vs. T2D and MD, and for association with T1D-onset age.
RESULTS: T1D-GRS2 outperformed T1D-SP-GRS for T1D vs. controls (AUC-ROC: 0.888 [95% CI: 0.867-0.908] vs. 0.837 [0.797-0.877], p=0.001), retaining high discrimination vs. T2D and MD (0.886 [0.865-0.907]). In the combined pediatric-onset T1D and control cohort, the P50 cutoff yielded a sensitivity of 0.80 (95% CI: 0.76-0.84) and specificity of 0.81 (0.77-0.84); P25 prioritized sensitivity (0.97 [0.95-0.99]) while P75 specificity (0.96 [0.93-0.97]). A P90 threshold conferred 26-fold higher T1D odds vs. controls, and 18- and 17-fold vs. T2D and MD (p <0.001). Higher T1D-GRS2 in childhood- vs. adulthood-onset T1D revealed an age-dependent risk profile primarily driven by HLA.
CONCLUSIONS: T1D-GRS2 discriminates T1D from other diabetes etiologies, providing a complementary tool to support diagnostic accuracy. The higher genetic risk associated with a younger age at onset provides key insights for early-stage T1D screening and intervention strategies.

title: Types 1 diabetes mellitus and Graves' disease in Sanjad-Sakati syndrome: a case report in Saudi Arabia.
abstract: Sanjad-Sakati syndrome (SSS) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by TBCE gene variants and characterized by congenital hypoparathyroidism, severe growth retardation, developmental delay, and dysmorphic features. We report a nine-year-old Saudi boy with genetically confirmed SSS due to a homozygous 12-bp deletion in exon 3 of the TBCE gene (c.155_166del12bp; p.S52_G55del), who presented with hypocalcemic convulsions at three weeks of age. At three years, he developed type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) with profound insulin deficiency and positive anti-islet cell and anti-GAD-65 antibodies. At four years, he developed Graves' disease, confirmed by hyperthyroidism, positive TSH receptor antibodies, and increased thyroid vascularity, followed by hypothyroidism requiring levothyroxine. Severe bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis was also identified. This case highlights the unusual coexistence of TBCE-related SSS, autoimmune T1DM, and Graves' disease, raising the possibility of potential immune dysregulation, although causality cannot be established. Longitudinal endocrine surveillance, particularly of thyroid function, may be warranted in patients with SSS.

title: Fertility preservation in girls and adolescents with Turner syndrome: lessons for reproductive care in differences of sex development - a mini-review.
abstract: Current knowledge regarding fertility preservation (FP) in girls is derived predominantly from pediatric oncology cohorts; however, FP is increasingly being applied to non-oncological conditions associated with impaired fertility, including differences of sex development (DSD). Turner syndrome (TS), characterized by accelerated germ cell depletion beginning during fetal life, represents the DSD condition with the greatest clinical experience in FP. This mini-review summarizes current evidence on ovarian tissue cryopreservation and oocyte cryopreservation in TS. Available data support the technical feasibility and general procedural safety of both approaches. A 46,XX cell line, spontaneous pubertal development, detectable AMH, and lower FSH concentrations are frequently associated with follicle detection or successful oocyte retrieval. However, evidence regarding utilization, pregnancy, and live birth remains very limited, and the reproductive effectiveness of FP in TS has not yet been established. Moreover, future cardiovascular eligibility for pregnancy and associated obstetric risks should be considered when counseling patients and families. Until long-term outcome data become available, individualized patient selection and multidisciplinary counseling are essential to provide realistic expectations regarding the potential benefits, limitations, and uncertainties of FP. Experience in TS may also inform reproductive care in other DSD conditions.

title: Pediatric prolactinoma-associated pituitary apoplexy presenting with acute visual loss: a case report, literature review, and management strategy.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Hemorrhagic pituitary apoplexy (PA) in children is exceedingly rare, with approximately 32 cases reported since 1980. Current guidelines recommend cabergoline as first-line therapy; however, acute complete visual loss mandates emergency surgical decompression. No guideline defines the optimal extent of resection, despite gross total resection carrying a 48-54 % risk of panhypopituitarism.
CASE PRESENTATION: An 11-year-old prepubertal girl presented with a 2-day history of complete right-eye visual loss. Serum prolactin was 987 μg/L, and MRI demonstrated a hemorrhagic sellar-suprasellar mass compressing the optic chiasm. Emergency endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery was performed with an intentionally limited strategy - hematoma evacuation, optic decompression, and partial debulking - deliberately avoiding aggressive capsular dissection. Histopathology confirmed prolactinoma. Vision was fully restored immediately after extubation, with near-complete visual field recovery on postoperative day 5 (VFI 98 %). Adrenocortical function was preserved. Central hypothyroidism developed, and levothyroxine was initiated. Cabergoline (0.25 mg/week) was started on postoperative day 5, achieving a 93.7 % prolactin reduction by day 20 (987 → 61.9 μg/L).
CONCLUSIONS: In pediatric prolactinoma-associated PA requiring emergency surgery, a decompression-first strategy prioritizing visual rescue and tissue diagnosis over gross total resection may reduce the risk of panhypopituitarism, with residual tumor subsequently managed with cabergoline. The rapid biochemical response documented here supports this approach, though multicenter prospective evaluation is required.

journal.title: Journal of pediatric endocrinology & metabolism : JPEM

title: Calcium Overload in Trisomy 21: An Underrecognized Cause of Persistent Hypercalcaemia - A Case Report.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Calcium overload in trisomy 21 is a rare and underrecognized cause of persistent parathyroid hormone (PTH)-independent hypercalcaemia in infants and young children with Down syndrome. Characteristic features include hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis, renal impairment, and failure to thrive. Delayed recognition may result in avoidable long-term complications.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 21-month-old boy with trisomy 21 presented with a six-month history of recurrent vomiting, feeding difficulties, and failure to thrive. Bilateral nephrocalcinosis was detected incidentally on abdominal ultrasound. Laboratory evaluation revealed marked hypercalcaemia with suppressed PTH and 1,25(OH)₂D, hypercalciuria, and acute kidney injury. Extensive diagnostic work-up excluded alternative causes of PTH-independent hypercalcaemia. Nutritional assessment showed an almost exclusively milk-based diet with minimal solid food intake. Initial treatment with intravenous fluids and a single dose of pamidronate resulted in only transient improvement. Following the diagnosis of calcium overload, a calcium-restricted diet consisting of normal and low-calcium formula was introduced and adjusted according to biochemical response. Serum calcium normalized and remained stable throughout 11 months of follow-up. Growth and developmental progress improved, while nephrocalcinosis persisted and renal function partially recovered.
CONCLUSION: Calcium overload in trisomy 21 should be considered in young children with Down syndrome presenting with failure to thrive, recurrent vomiting, and nephrocalcinosis in combination with PTH-independent hypercalcemia. Early recognition and initiation of dietary calcium restriction may prevent long-term complications such as chronic kidney disease and prolonged growth impairment.

title: Early-Life Presentation and Phenotypic Variability of the IGF1R c.3595G>A (p.Gly1199Arg) Variant: A Case Report.
abstract: Most infants born small for gestational age (SGA) achieve spontaneous catch-up growth within the first two years of life; however, a subset remains growth-restricted and warrants further evaluation. Persistent short stature accompanied by microcephaly should prompt consideration of an underlying monogenic disorder. We report a term male infant born with severe SGA (birth weight -3.8 SDS; birth length -2.2 SDS) and microcephaly. At 16 months of age, his height was -2.7 SDS and head circumference -3.1 SDS. Initial insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) concentration was mildly decreased (-1.0 SDS) with normal insulin-like growth factor binding protein-3 (IGFBP-3, +1.0 SDS). Following nutritional optimization, IGF-1 increased to supranormal levels (+2.0 SDS), yet linear growth remained persistently below -2 SDS without sustained catch-up. Genetic analysis identified a heterozygous IGF1R c.3595G>A (p.Gly1199Arg) variant inherited from his short-statured mother. The variant was absent in population databases, localized within the intracellular tyrosine kinase domain, and predicted to be deleterious by multiple in silico tools (REVEL 0.98; AlphaMissense 1.0), supporting likely pathogenic classification. Previously reported individuals carrying this variant were evaluated later in childhood or adolescence. This case represents the earliest documented presentation and highlights a biochemical-auxological dissociation characterized by elevated IGF-1 levels without proportional linear growth, consistent with impaired receptor-mediated signaling. This report broadens the phenotypic and temporal spectrum of the IGF1R Gly1199Arg variant and underscores the importance of early molecular evaluation in SGA infants with persistent microcephaly and inadequate catch-up growth.

journal.title: Journal of clinical research in pediatric endocrinology

title: Reconsidering the Interpretation of Thyroid Cancer Risk in Pediatric Hashimoto Thyroiditis.
Clinical and Genetic Heterogeneity of Triple A Syndrome: A Multicenter Study.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Triple A syndrome (AAAS) is a rare autosomal recessive neuroendocrine disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the AAAS gene and characterized by marked clinical heterogeneity.
METHODS: In this multicenter retrospective study, we analyzed 23 patients from 18 families diagnosed across 9 centers in Türkiye to characterize the molecular and clinical features of AAAS. Six distinct variants in the AAAS gene were identified in this cohort, with truncating variants predominating.
RESULTS: The most frequent variant was c.1066_1067delCT (p.Leu356Valfs*8), detected in 7 of 18 families, followed by the nonsense variant c.1432C>T (p.Arg478*), identified in 6 families. Clinically, the most common initial presenting complaints were alacrima (6/23), achalasia (5/23), and adrenal insufficiency (4/23). Cumulative assessment during follow-up revealed the complete classical triad in 15/23 patients. Neurological involvement was frequent and showed an age-dependent pattern, with manifestations such as dysarthria (5/23) and autonomic dysfunction including anhidrosis (7/23); gait disturbance (8/23) was also commonly observed. Other frequent clinical findings included hyperpigmentation (12/23), short stature (11/23), palmoplantar hyperkeratosis (6/23), and microcephaly (4/23). Mineralocorticoid deficiency was reported in 7/23 patients based on physician documentation, six of whom had concomitant glucocorticoid deficiency.
CONCLUSION: This multicenter cohort highlights the marked clinical variability of AAAS, including progressive neurological involvement and heterogeneity in the recognition and biochemical presentation of mineralocorticoid dysfunction.

title: The predictive value of glycated CD59 for fetal overgrowth in second-trimester pregnant women.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To investigate the predictive value of glycated CD59 (gCD59) during mid-pregnancy for adverse pregnancy outcomes, specifically macrosomia and large for gestational age (LGA), in a prospective cohort of pregnant women undergoing oral glucose tolerance testing (OGTT), with adjustment for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) status.
METHODS: A total of 672 pregnant women who attended prenatal visits at the Affiliated Suqian Hospital of Xuzhou Medical University from January 2022 to July 2023 were enrolled, and baseline data were collected via the Zhendings Maternal and Child Health System. At 24-28 weeks of gestation, an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) was performed. Based on the results, participants were divided into a GDM group and a normal glucose tolerance (NGT) group for descriptive comparisons; for all predictive analyses, GDM status was included as a covariate in multivariable models. Concurrently, gCD59 levels were measured using the ELISA method. The pregnant women were followed up until after delivery, and data on delivery-related information and pregnancy outcomes were collected. Differences in pregnancy outcomes between the two groups were compared. Logistic regression analysis was used to identify risk factors for adverse pregnancy outcomes, and the predictive value of gCD59 levels for adverse pregnancy outcomes was assessed using ROC curves.
RESULTS: Macrosomia and Large for Gestational Age (LGA) were the two most common adverse pregnancy outcomes. Compared with the NGT group, the incidence of macrosomia and LGA was significantly higher in the GDM group (P < 0.05). Compared with the NGT group, gCD59 levels were significantly higher in the GDM group (1.49 (0.90, 2.33) vs. 0.87 (0.39, 1.62), P < 0.001). Logistic regression analysis indicated that gCD59 was an independent risk factor for macrosomia and LGA, and the incidence of macrosomia and LGA increased with rising gCD59 levels. In predictive modeling, the addition of gCD59 to traditional risk factors improved the AUC for macrosomia from 0.770 (95% CI: 0.679-0.833) to 0.864 (95% CI: 0.823-0.904) (DeLong P = 0.046); for LGA, the AUC improved from 0.723 (95% CI: 0.663-0.782) to 0.790 (95% CI: 0.737-0.843) (DeLong P = 0.103).
CONCLUSION: Macrosomia and LGA were the most common adverse pregnancy outcomes in the study cohort. gCD59 was identified as an independent risk factor for both macrosomia and LGA. In predictive modeling, gCD59 demonstrated statistically significant incremental value for macrosomia (AUC: 0.770 vs. 0.864, DeLong P = 0.046), while for LGA the improvement showed a favorable trend but did not reach statistical significance (AUC: 0.723 vs. 0.790, DeLong P = 0.103). These findings suggest that gCD59 may serve as a supplementary biomarker, particularly for risk stratification of macrosomia, with potential utility for identifying pregnancies at risk of excessive fetal growth.

title: Recurring and isolated intronic FGFR1 variants as an underdiagnosed cause of congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH) is a genetically heterogeneous disorder characterized by absent or delayed puberty and infertility due to gonadotropin-releasing hormone deficiency. While loss-of-function variants in FGFR1 are the most commonly known genetic cause of CHH, diagnostic screening typically focuses on coding exons, potentially overlooking pathogenic variants in noncoding regions.
METHODS: We investigated 4 unrelated families with CHH. Family 1 included a mother and 3 daughters presenting with variable reproductive phenotypes and incomplete penetrance of anosmia; Family 3 consisted of a girl with CHH and anosmia; and Families 2 and 4 consisted of male patients who presented with CHH and anosmia. Genetic investigations were done using either exome or genome sequencing. Experimental characterization of the identified intronic variants was conducted using RNA extracted from peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Exome or genome sequencing-based haplotyping was performed for the recurring variant.
RESULTS: In Families 1 to 3, we identified a recurring heterozygous intronic variant in FGFR1: c.92-19G > A. RNA analysis confirmed that this variant generates a cryptic splice acceptor site, leading to the inclusion of 17 intronic nucleotides, resulting in a premature stop codon. Haplotype analysis revealed the variant occurred independently in each family. In Family 4, a distinct heterozygous intronic variant was identified in FGFR1, which was shown to cause intron 15 retention with premature termination.
CONCLUSION: Our findings demonstrate that intronic variants in FGFR1 are a possible cause of CHH and can lead to diverse clinical phenotypes ranging from normosmic CHH to severe Kallmann syndrome, including significant presentation in female patients.

title: Impact of antenatal corticosteroid exposure on glycemic control in preterm infants assessed by continuous glucose monitoring: preliminary results from a single center study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Antenatal corticosteroids (ACS) are routinely administered to women at risk of preterm delivery to improve neonatal respiratory outcomes. However, ACS exposure has been associated with neonatal hypoglycemia, and its impact on overall glycemic control and variability-particularly at earlier gestational ages-remains incompletely defined.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate glycemic control using continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in preterm infants exposed to ACS and to assess the influence of timing of administration and gestational age on glycemic patterns.
METHODS: This prospective single-center cohort study included preterm infants born at <35 weeks of gestation and admitted to a level III neonatal intensive care unit between February 2023 and August 2024. Infants were classified according to ACS exposure as complete course, partial course, or no exposure. CGM was performed during the first 48 hours of life. Hypoglycemic (<45 mg/dL) and hyperglycemic (>180 mg/dL) events, as well as glycemic variability assessed by the mean amplitude of glycemic excursions (MAGE), were analyzed. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on the interval between ACS administration and delivery (≤7 days vs >7 days) and gestational age (<34 vs ≥34 weeks). Statistical significance was adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure.
RESULTS: Sixty-four infants were included (41 complete ACS, 15 partial ACS, 8 no ACS). Baseline characteristics were comparable among groups. During the first day of life, hypoglycemic events occurred exclusively in infants exposed to a complete course of ACS (p = 0.005), predominantly in those exposed within seven days prior to delivery. This difference was not observed on the second day. Hyperglycemic events were significantly more frequent in infants born before 34 weeks of gestation (p = 0.005). Glycemic variability, assessed by MAGE, did not differ significantly according to ACS exposure, timing, or gestational age.
CONCLUSIONS: Exposure to a complete and recent course of ACS is associated with an increased risk of early neonatal hypoglycemia in preterm infants, particularly within the first 24 hours of life. CGM enables detailed assessment of glycemic instability and may support improved metabolic monitoring in this high-risk population.

title: Diabetes Distress in Caregivers of Young Children With Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The American Diabetes Association recommends screening for diabetes distress in individuals with diabetes and their caregivers. We evaluated the clinical utility of the Problem Areas in Diabetes-Parent Revised version (PAID-PR) distress screener in caregivers of young children with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) and examined associations between diabetes distress, demographic and clinical characteristics, and diabetes technology use.
METHODS: In this prospective survey study, caregivers of children with T1DM aged <8 years completed the PAID-PR during multidisciplinary diabetes clinic visits. The PAID-PR scores and clinical data were collected. Associations between diabetes distress, clinical characteristics, and diabetes technology use were assessed using the Fisher exact, Wilcoxon rank sum, and 2-sample t tests. Distress related to theoretical vs immediate burdens was compared using paired t tests.
RESULTS: Thirty caregivers (73.3% mothers) of children with T1DM (mean age [SD] = 5.4y [1.9], 70% non-Hispanic White, 60% commercially insured) completed the PAID-PR. Child median diabetes duration was 1.5 years (interquartile range [IQR] = 0.6, 2.3), median HbA1c 7.6% (IQR = 6.9, 8.1). All children used continuous glucose monitors, 73.3% Omnipod 5, 6.7% Tandem Mobi, and 20% multiple daily injections. The median distress score was 30.6/100 (IQR = 22.2, 36.1; the lowest 75th percentile of distress = 24.3 [12.5, 31.9]; the highest 25th percentile = 42.9 [38.6, 52.8]). Scores did not differ by demographics, clinical characteristics, or diabetes technology use. Caregivers indicated significantly greater distress from theoretical vs immediate burdens (P < .0001).
CONCLUSIONS: Caregivers of young children with T1DM experience greater distress related to anticipated future (theoretical) burdens than with immediate diabetes management. Understanding these distress patterns can help guide psychosocial supports.

title: Delayed diagnosis of familial glucocorticoid deficiency type 4 in a child with epilepsy: a case report and literature review.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Familial glucocorticoid deficiency type 4 (FGD4) is a rare autosomal recessive form of primary adrenal insufficiency caused by biallelic variants in the NNT gene and characterized predominantly by isolated glucocorticoid deficiency. Neurological presentations may obscure the underlying adrenal disorder. We describe a pediatric case with a novel NNT variant not previously associated with FGD4 and review the reported clinical and genetic spectrum.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 10-year-old girl presented with a 4-year history of epilepsy and longstanding diffuse hyperpigmentation. A homozygous frameshift variant in NNT (c.645delT; p.Phe215Leufs*17) was identified in the appendix to the previous whole-exome sequencing report and confirmed by Sanger sequencing; both parents were heterozygous carriers. The variant was classified as pathogenic according to ACMG criteria. The patient also had primary hypothyroidism, symptomatic epilepsy, and metabolic encephalopathy. During follow-up with glucocorticoid and thyroxine replacement therapy and continued antiepileptic treatment seizure frequency decreased, hyperpigmentation improved, and communication, attention, and social interaction improved.
CONCLUSIONS: This case expands the mutational spectrum of NNT-related FGD4 and emphasizes the importance of considering adrenal insufficiency in pediatric patients presenting with seizures and hyperpigmentation. Early recognition and diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency enable timely hormone replacement therapy and may reduce the risk of neurological and metabolic complications.

title: Early-onset obesity and growth failure in children with pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A: reference growth and weight curves from a Polish cohort.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate longitudinal growth and weight patterns in children with pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP1A) and provide disease-specific growth and weight curves to aid clinical monitoring.
METHODS: Retrospective analysis of 26 children (12 girls and 14 boys) from 18 families, including 25 patients with PHP1A and one patient with PHP1B; 19 patients had genetically confirmed PHP1A. Height and weight measurements were analyzed using quantile regression to generate centile charts. The patient with PHP1B was excluded from growth-trend analyses. Biochemical and hormonal parameters were assessed.
RESULTS: PHP1A was diagnosed at a median age of 6.1 years. Growth deceleration became evident after age 8, with a median final height of 147.7 cm (-2.5 SDS) for girls and 156 cm (-2.9 SDS) for boys. Body weight was above the 97th percentile until age 10, with partial normalization during adolescence. No correlation was observed between biochemical or hormonal parameters and obesity. Growth and weight patterns were consistent with findings from larger international cohorts.
CONCLUSIONS: Children with PHP1A show early-onset obesity and growth deceleration after age 8. Disease-specific centile charts may provide a practical tool for monitoring growth and weight trajectories in this population. Early clinical assessment and individualized interventions are recommended.

title: Amino Acid Profiles Distinguish Glycemic Phenotypes in Childhood and Predict 10-Year Risk of Dysglycemia in Young Adults: The BCAMS Study.
abstract: Prospective evidence linking childhood amino acid (AA) dysregulation with future diabetes risk remains limited. We examined whether AA profiles distinguished childhood glycemic phenotypes and predicted dysglycemia risk in the Beijing Children and Adolescents Metabolic Syndrome (BCAMS) cohort. AA alterations were already detectable in children with normoglycemia and insulin resistance; six AAs were associated with 10-year dysglycemia risk, and their addition to clinical variables improved prediction. Ile showed the largest estimated indirect association with incident dysglycemia through follow-up insulin resistance; dietary Ile restriction in obese mice produced concordant metabolic changes, supporting AA profiling for early risk identification and Ile as a candidate modifiable target.
